title: A Rare Family of Barn Owls Moves Into Manhattan
summary:
New Yorkers have some surprising new neighbors. A family of barn owls has made its home in a water tower on top of a building on West 75th Street, close to Central Park in Manhattan.

According to Andrew Farnsworth, a scientist who studies bird migration at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, this is the first time barn owls are known to have nested in Manhattan in recorded history. "It was, like, totally shocking," he said.

Word of the owls spread after Elisabeth Williams, a neighbor, told a local news outlet on October 6 that she and her husband had seen several owls at the water tower. "In a place like Manhattan, you normally really have to go out of your way to encounter nature," she said.

David Barrett, a birder who runs the social media account Manhattan Bird Alert, said he has seen at least one adult owl and five young owls, called fledglings. People believe there are two adults. He has also seen an adult carrying food back to the tower.

Barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, the city's parks department says. New York is at the northern edge of where barn owls live, and the state's environmental agency says their numbers have dropped over time.

Now crowds gather each night hoping to spot the birds. "They're magical, they're nocturnal, they are secretive," said Jessica Wilson of the NYC Bird Alliance.

Before anyone knew about the owls, neighbors heard loud screeching at night starting in September. Farnsworth said that screech is how barn owls talk to one another. One neighbor, Thomas Obersteiner, now lets nature photographers watch from his roof deck. Williams says the experience may turn her family into bird watchers. "I think we're about to become birders," she said.
why_it_matters: Wild animals can find homes even in big cities, and their numbers in New York have dropped, so a rare nest gives people a chance to learn about and protect them.

background_read: Barn owls are pale owls with heart-shaped faces that hunt small animals, mostly at night.
They often nest in quiet, high, sheltered places such as barns, hollow trees or towers.
Many buildings in New York City have wooden water towers on their roofs, which can offer birds a sheltered spot.
Bird watchers and scientists keep records of sightings, which is how experts know whether a species has nested somewhere before.
